intro: Teaching in the S4E lab follows the same idea as the research: students learn to compute, to reason about materials, and to check a numerical result against physics before trusting it. The courses below are taught at Johns Hopkins University. The workshops, outreach programs, and research mentoring extend the same material to people outside the classroom.

courses.title: Materials Modeling
text: Students write scientific code in Python and use it to model materials. The course starts with the tools of the trade: the UNIX shell, Git, LaTeX, and Make. It then builds numerical methods from their mathematical statements, including integration of equations of motion, relaxation methods for fields, eigenvalue problems, random numbers, and Monte Carlo sampling. Those methods are applied to materials through density functional theory, high-throughput materials databases, molecular dynamics, and machine learning. The final unit is autonomous experimentation, in which prior results choose the next experiment, built on the LEGOLAS low-cost autonomous laboratory kit.

There are no written examinations. Each of the seven assignments is a working program and a report typeset in LaTeX, tracked in a GitHub repository, and the semester ends with a group project presented in class. Students implement each method themselves rather than calling a library that already solves the problem, and every result is checked against an analytic limit, a conservation law, or a convergence test. The density functional theory, high-throughput modeling, and molecular dynamics assignments run on the university's research computing cluster.
The course enrolls 15 to 17 students each fall, most of them graduate students in materials science and related departments, with a waiting list in 2026.

courses.title: Gateway Computing: Python
text: The first programming course for engineering students: algorithms, control structures, functions, files, testing, and debugging, with problems drawn from engineering and science. Corey teaches two sections each spring, 20 to 30 students in total.

courses.title: Research for credit
text: Undergraduate, master's, and graduate students carry out research in the group for course credit during the academic year and over the summer. How to join is on the Jobs page.

workshops_text: The group organizes hands-on workshops at Johns Hopkins University on data-driven materials modeling, quantum computing for materials, and moving energy research toward application. Recordings and notebooks from past events are on the Workshops page. Corey co-organized schools on high-throughput computational materials science at Carnegie Mellon University, the University of Pennsylvania, Texas A&M University, TU Dresden, and the University of Rwanda. He has presented at the University of Maryland and NIST Machine Learning for Materials Research bootcamps since 2018.

outreach.title: Research in the group
outreach.text: Since 2022 the group has hosted nine undergraduate researchers, six high school researchers, five visiting students, and four master's students alongside its PhD students, postdoctoral associates, and research scientists. Undergraduates join through the ROSETAS REU summer program and through Johns Hopkins University research credit. Several undergraduate and high school researchers are co-authors on group publications.

outreach.title: Ingenuity Project research practicum
outreach.text: Since 2023 the group has mentored high school students from the Ingenuity Project at Baltimore Polytechnic Institute in its year-long Research Practicum. Students build and program the LEGOLAS low-cost autonomous laboratory, a LEGO-based robot that runs experiments and uses machine learning to choose the next one, and each cohort trains the one that follows. The same kit, developed at the University of Maryland and NIST, closes the Materials Modeling course each year.
